usage: The standard toast as everyone raises glasses

Formal toast, often led by the boss after a short speech
'One shot' — drink the whole glass in one go (English loan)

Okay, everyone, cheers!
자 ('alright') gathers attention right before the toast
오늘 고생하셨습니다. 건배!
You all worked hard today. Cheers!
A short line of appreciation typically precedes the toast
팀장님이 건배 제의 하셨어요.
The team leader proposed a toast.
건배 제의(를) 하다 = 'to propose a toast', what the senior does

The English-speaker pitfall is the drinking posture, not the word: with a senior present you hold your glass slightly lower than theirs when clinking and often turn your head away to drink — saying 건배 perfectly but clinking above the boss's glass reads as rude. usage: Polite; asking the server or your neighbor to pour
반말, to a close coworker or friend
Let me pour you one more
Offering to fill SOMEONE ELSE'S glass (honorific)

One more glass of soju here, please.
Naming the drink (소주) makes the order clear to staff
한 잔 더 하실래요?
Would you like one more?
Offering to a senior; -ㄹ래요 invites without pressure
저 한 잔만 더 하고 일어날게요.
I'll have just one more and then head out.
일어나다 ('to get up') politely signals you'll leave soon
nuance: 한 잔 더 is 한 ('one', native number) + 잔 (counter for cups/glasses) + 더 ('more'), the core phrase for another round. Crucially the counter 잔 takes NATIVE numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — '두 잔' not '이 잔' is a constant learner slip. Watch the direction of the favor verb: 주세요 ('please give') asks someone to pour FOR YOU, while 받으세요 ('please receive') is what you say while pouring for THEM — mixing these flips who's serving whom. The near-synonym 한 잔 더 할게요 uses 하다 ('to do/have a drink') to announce you'll have another yourself, vs. 주세요 which requests it; both are natural. The English-speaker pitfall is the pouring etiquette around this phrase: in Korea you generally don't refill your OWN glass — you pour for others and they pour for you — so loudly asking 한 잔 더 주세요 while topping up only yourself can look slightly off; better to offer 한 잔 더 받으세요 to your neighbor or let a junior notice your empty glass. Also receive a poured drink with two hands from a senior.

english: Let me pour you a drink
usage: Let me pour you a glass
Polite-humble; offering to pour for a senior
반말, to a friend or close junior
Allow me to pour you one (formal)
Very deferential, to a boss/elder at a formal table
Short prompt as you tilt the bottle toward their glass
examples: 부장님, 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요.
Director, let me pour you a glass.
Address the senior by title first, then offer
잔 비셨네요. 제가 따라 드릴게요.
Your glass is empty — let me fill it.
잔(이) 비다 ('the glass is empty') is the cue to pour
두 손으로 따라 드리는 게 예의예요.
Pouring with both hands is the polite way.
두 손으로 ('with both hands') is essential toward elders

The honorific machinery is the whole point: you use 드리다 (humble give) because you're serving up to someone higher, whereas to a friend you'd swap to plain 주다 → 따라 줄게. Don't confuse 따르다 ('to pour') with 따르다 meaning 'to follow' — same spelling, but context (a bottle and a glass) makes it 'pour'. The most formal version 한 잔 올리겠습니다 uses 올리다 ('to raise up/offer'), reserved for bosses and elders. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: forgetting both-hands etiquette (hold the bottle with your right hand and support your right forearm or the bottle with your left), and over-pouring to the brim — fill soju/beer about 80-90%, not overflowing. Also, you POUR for others and let them pour for you; pouring your own is avoided. Saying this line while topping up only yourself defeats its purpose.

english: Your glass is empty — here, let me pour you one

Polite; noticing and offering to refill a senior
Your glass is empty — take one
Please allow me to pour you one
Please top up my glass too
채우다 ('to fill'); inviting them to pour back
examples: 부장님, 잔 비었네요. 한 잔 받으세요.
Director, your glass is empty — let me pour you one.
Spot the empty glass and offer; 받으세요 = 'please receive'
어, 잔 비었네. 내가 한 잔 따라 줄게.
Oh, your glass is empty — I'll pour you one.
Casual peer version with 따라 주다
계속 비어 있길래 한 잔 채워 드렸어요.
It was sitting empty, so I filled it up for you.

You then say 한 잔 받으세요 (받다 'receive' + honorific 으세요), literally 'please receive one', the set phrase said WHILE pouring into someone's glass. This whole move is central 회식 etiquette: you watch others' glasses, and when one empties you offer to fill it — you do NOT just refill your own. The direction of verbs is the trap: 받으세요 ('please receive') is for the person whose glass YOU are filling, while 주세요 ('please give') is when you want THEM to pour for you — beginners flip these. 비다 is intransitive ('to be/become empty'), so it's 잔이 비다 / 잔 비었어요, not 잔을 비우다 (which is the transitive 비우다 'to empty', as in 잔을 비우다 = 'drain your glass', a different, more aggressive 'bottoms up' meaning). Stating 'your glass is empty' without offering.

usage: Polite; explaining you can't drink much
-는 편이다 softens it to 'tend to be'
You can hold your liquor (high tolerance)
The opposite: 세다 ('strong'), said of a strong drinker
examples: 저는 술이 약해서 조금만 마실게요.
I have a low tolerance, so I'll only drink a little.
약해서 ('because weak') gives a polite reason to go slow
술이 약하셔서 천천히 드세요.
You're a lightweight, so pace yourself.
Said kindly to someone who flushes/tires fast
제가 술이 약한 편이라 한 잔이면 얼굴 빨개져요.
I'm rather a lightweight, so one glass turns my face red.
얼굴(이) 빨개지다 ('face turns red') is a classic tell
nuance: 술이 약해요 is 술 ('alcohol') + 이 (subject marker) + 약하다 ('to be weak'), i.e. 'my alcohol(-tolerance) is weak' — the polite, face-saving way to say you can't drink much before anyone over-pours for you. The opposite is 술이 세요 (세다 = 'strong'), said of a heavy drinker. The PARTICLE is the classic trap: it's 술'이' 약하다 (subject), describing the alcohol/tolerance as weak — learners wrongly say 술'을' 약해요 with the object marker, which is ungrammatical because 약하다 is a descriptive adjective, not a transitive verb. Don't 직역 'I am weak to alcohol' into 저는 술에 약해요 — while 에 is occasionally heard, the natural set phrase is 술이 약해요. Distinguish this from 술을 못 마셔요 ('I can't drink at all'): 약하다 means low tolerance (you drink a little), while 못 마시다 means you don't/can't drink — saying 약해요 still implies you'll have some. Sorry, I can't drink — I'll have cider instead.

체질상 술을 못 마셔요.
I can't drink for constitutional reasons.
체질상 ('due to my constitution') is a respected, unarguable reason
저 술 못 마시는데 분위기는 맞출게요.

usage: Polite; asking for a small pour

Ah, just to there — thank you.
거기까지만요 stops the pour at the current level

I'll step out for some air

대리 부르기 전에 술 좀 깨려고요.

usage: Polite-casual; offering to pay for everyone
한턱내다 ('treat to a meal'), a touch warmer/idiomatic
살게요 ('I'll buy'); offering to pay later

An occasion (promotion) is the classic reason to treat
오늘 제가 살 테니까 마음껏 드세요.
It's on me today, so eat all you want.
마음껏 드세요 ('help yourself freely') pairs with treating
에이, 오늘은 제가 쏠게요. 다음에 사 주세요.

usage: I think I'm a little tipsy
Honestly admitting a buzz; -ㄴ 것 같다 softens
Said to someone else who's had too much

I'm really not drunk — I can have one more.
진짜 ('really') emphasizes the reassurance
살짝 취한 것 같긴 한데 괜찮아요.

살짝 ('slightly') is an honest middle-ground admission
취해서 실수할까 봐 이제 그만 마실게요.

Yesterday's drinks still haven't worn off

My head feels like it's splitting

I overdid it yesterday, so my hangover is terrible.
과음하다 ('to drink too much') is the cause of 숙취
숙취 때문에 아침에 아무것도 못 먹었어요.

숙취엔 꿀물이나 해장국이 최고예요.
For a hangover, honey water or haejang soup is the best.
